statement: In a class of 30 students, 18 are in the chess club, 15 are in the choir and 4 are in neither. How many students are in exactly one of the two?

choices.misconception: I found the number of students in both, 7, and gave that instead of the number in exactly one.
I found the students in the chess club only, 18 - 7 = 11, and forgot those in the choir only.
I gave the number in at least one of the two, 30 - 4 = 26, which still includes the students in both.
I added 18 and 15 without noticing that some students were counted twice.

hints: First find how many students are in at least one of the two.
Students in at least one group: the total minus those in neither. Compare this with 18 + 15 to find how many were counted twice, which is the number in both.
26 students are in at least one group, and 18 + 15 = 33, so 7 are in both.

solutions.reliable: 30 - 4 = 26 students are in at least one group. Adding 18 + 15 = 33 counts the students in both groups twice, so 33 - 26 = 7 are in both. In exactly one group: 26 - 7 = 19. Check: chess only is 18 - 7 = 11 and choir only is 15 - 7 = 8, and 11 + 8 = 19. The transferable idea: inclusion-exclusion gives the overlap, and exactly one means at least one minus both.
solutions.elegant: Exactly one = (18 + 15) - 2 x 7 = 19, because the students in both groups appear twice in 33 and must be removed completely.

whyOnTest: Two-set counting hinges on the overlap, and this question asks for exactly one, so every intermediate count appears among the choices.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
